content: Adapting global health guidelines to national programs is a complex process that requires expertise in local health conditions, behaviors, and cultural contexts. When incorporating guidelines on contraceptive use into national sexual and reproductive health programs, it is essential to recognize that these are not merely documents to be distributed. Instead, they represent healthcare practices that must be introduced to providers through a structured process of adaptation and implementation. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides guidance for countries on integrating sexual and reproductive health guidelines into national programs, as outlined in the publication Introducing WHO’s Sexual and Reproductive Health Guidelines and Tools into National Programs. This document is intended for policymakers, program managers, and healthcare professionals who aim to implement evidence-based practices in sexual and reproductive health. The WHO recommends six overarching principles for effectively adapting and implementing sexual and reproductive health guidelines into national programs. These principles include building consensus, leveraging existing resources, identifying barriers and facilitators, ensuring evidence-based adaptations, planning for scale-up from the outset, and implementing interventions to change provider practices. To introduce the third edition of the Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use, WHO suggests a six-step process: planning advocacy, conducting a situational analysis, adapting the guidance to the country’s needs, designing an implementation strategy, pilot-testing and evaluating, and implementing advocacy and scaling up. This process may vary depending on whether the guidance is being introduced for the first time or used to update existing guidelines. Collaboration and participation among policymakers, professional bodies, and national experts are critical to fostering ownership and acceptance of the guidelines. For individuals with disabilities, the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) mandates equal access to sexual and reproductive healthcare. However, healthcare providers often fail to offer these services due to misconceptions about the sexual activity of people with disabilities. Providing contraceptive services to individuals with disabilities requires careful consideration of their preferences, the nature of their disability, and the specifics of different contraceptive methods. For example, barrier methods may be challenging for those with limited manual dexterity, and combined oral contraceptives may not be suitable for women with impaired circulation or immobile extremities due to the risk of deep vein thrombosis. Additionally, individuals with intellectual or mental health disabilities who struggle with daily medication adherence may benefit from alternative methods. For women with difficulties managing menstrual hygiene, the impact of contraceptive methods on menstrual cycles should also be considered. All medical decisions must be based on informed choice, supported by adequate sexual and reproductive health education. Adolescents in many countries face significant barriers to accessing contraceptive information and services, which are essential for protecting their sexual and reproductive health and rights. Programs must address these barriers and meet the contraceptive needs of adolescents. Adolescents are generally eligible to use all contraceptive methods available to adults, and age alone should not be a reason to deny any method. Concerns about specific methods, such as progestogen-only injectables for those under 18, must be weighed against the benefits of preventing unintended pregnancies. Adolescents, regardless of marital status, have the right to privacy and confidentiality in health matters, including reproductive healthcare. Services should be accessible without requiring parental or guardian authorization. Social and behavioral factors, such as sporadic sexual activity and the need to conceal contraceptive use, should also be considered when selecting methods for adolescents. Expanding the range of contraceptive options can improve satisfaction, acceptance, and usage rates. Proper education and counseling before and during method selection can help adolescents make informed and voluntary decisions. Intrauterine devices (IUDs) are long-acting contraceptive methods suitable for most women, including adolescents and those who have not given birth. However, IUDs do not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV. In cases of STI/HIV risk, consistent and correct condom use is recommended. Copper-bearing IUDs (Cu-IUDs) and levonorgestrel-releasing IUDs (LNG-IUDs) can be initiated at various times, depending on the individual’s menstrual cycle, postpartum status, or post-abortion status. For emergency contraception, Cu-IUDs can be inserted within five days of unprotected intercourse. LNG-IUDs are not recommended for emergency contraception due to insufficient evidence of their safety and effectiveness in this context. Before IUD insertion, essential examinations include a pelvic/genital examination and STI risk assessment. Prophylactic antibiotics are generally not recommended for routine IUD insertion, except in settings with a high prevalence of cervical gonococcal and chlamydial infections and limited STI screening. Women should be counseled to monitor for symptoms of pelvic inflammatory disease, especially during the first month of use. Menstrual abnormalities, such as spotting or heavier bleeding, are common during the first 3–6 months of IUD use. These issues are usually not harmful and tend to decrease over time. Treatment options, such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or tranexamic acid, may be offered during bleeding days. Aspirin should not be used. If bleeding persists or becomes unacceptable, the IUD can be removed, and alternative contraceptive methods can be explored. To prevent anemia, iron supplementation or dietary advice may be provided.
